quote: Bayesian probability theory is the quantitative logic of which Aristotle’s qualitative logic is a special case
content: Syllogistic is monadic predicate logic, and monadic logic reduces to propositional logic about an arbitrary individual. Probability theory has a standard treatment of it: read "All A are B" as P(B|A) = 1 and "Some A are B" as P(B|A) > 0. On that reading Barbara is a theorem of the probability calculus, since P(C|A) = 1 whenever P(B|A) = 1 and P(C|B) = 1. The other valid moods follow in the same way as limiting cases, while the calculus also handles "most" and "few," which Aristotle could not. Oaksford and Chater built their account of human syllogistic reasoning on exactly this reading of the quantifiers (Chater & Oaksford 1999). "Special case" is a checkable claim, and it checks out.

quote: Actually, I think Shermer’s falling prey to correspondence bias by supposing that there’s any particular correlation between Rand’s philosophy and the way her followers formed a cult.
content: The essay rejects one mechanism, Shermer's, which was that Rand believed certainty possible. It rejects it with a clean counterexample: chemists are certain of atomic theory and have not become a cult. The sense-of-life doctrine Fable proposes is a different mechanism, and the dates are awkward for it. The Romantic Manifesto collects essays from the late 1960s. The Strauss anecdote and the formation of the Collective are from the 1950s. A doctrine that turns the leader's dislikes into metaphysical diagnoses, written after the dislikes began, fits the essay's account: "All sorts of excellent justifications somehow leap to mind." "Every cause wants to be a cult" also does not say that doctrines never matter. Cultish Countercultishness lists doctrinal risk factors. The claim is that no doctrine gives immunity, and one praising "reason" gave none.
